tagline.text: A calm lake in Camalig that mirrors Mayon Volcano

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–800 (entrance, activities and meals, per person)

children.text: Sumlang Lake is a small lake of about 14 hectares in Camalig, Albay, loved for the view of Mayon Volcano reflected on its still water. It is a good place to spend half a day on a bamboo raft, a kayak or a floating cottage.

Sumlang Lake is a small lake in the village of Sumlang in Camalig, Albay. One blogger gives its area as about 14 hectares. Mayon Volcano stands beyond the lake with nothing blocking the view, and on calm early mornings the cone-shaped volcano is reflected upside down on the water, which is the scene most visitors come for. It is about
15–20 minutes
by car from central Legazpi, and one guide says it is about
5 minutes
from the Camalig town proper, so it is easy to combine with Hoyop-Hoyopan Cave or Cagsawa Ruins in a single day.

The lake's present look is the result of work by local residents. A 2016 blog says the lake was once covered in water lilies and that its calm surface appeared after villagers cleared them. The same review credits Felipe Napa, a local business owner who is also the village chief, with leading the effort, and says about
300–500 people

visited on weekends. A bamboo raft race was reportedly held in 2014. Facilities appear to have grown since then, and a 2025 guide describes an entrance fee, bamboo rafts, kayaks, aqua bikes, fish feeding and floating cottages.

Sumlang Lake is for sightseeing and light water activities, not swimming. The 2025 guide says swimming is not allowed and recommends wearing a life jacket on the rafts, kayaks and aqua bikes. The lake is not large, so you can see all of it in an hour or two. It is therefore better as a half-day stop linked with other sights in Camalig and Legazpi than as a standalone destination.

Mayon cannot be seen on cloudy days, and in the heat of the day ripples can blur the reflection. The best time is early on a dry-season morning. Fees and opening hours have changed from year to year, so check the latest announcements before you go. Reviews quote very different prices, so the safest approach is to go by the posted rates on site.

On a windless early morning in the dry season, the cone-shaped Mayon Volcano is mirrored upside down on the lake. If photography is your goal, arrive early. On cloudy days the volcano may not be visible. One reviewer notes that the lake sits right in front of Mayon, so the view is open.

There is reportedly a café in front of the lake that serves Bicolano dishes such as laing, Bicol Express and pancit Bato. Check the menu and prices on site.

blocks.title: A sight built by the villagers

children.text: This place reflects the effort of villagers who cleared the water lilies and developed the facilities. Please respect the posted rules and rates.
Guides mention that Cagsawa Ruins, Quitinday Hills, the Mayon Skyline View Deck and Daraga Church are nearby. You can see several places in one outing, which is efficient.

items.title: Morning half day
items.subtitle: A plan aimed at the Mayon reflection

children.text: From Friday to Sunday, arrive when the lake opens. One guide says it opens at 8:00 on weekdays. Early hours have less wind and a clearer Mayon.
Pay the entrance and environmental fees, then photograph Mayon's reflection from the shore first.
Take a raft or a kayak. The view of Mayon from the middle of the lake is the best.
Have a combined breakfast and lunch of Bicolano dishes at the café by the lake.
Take a tricycle to Camalig town or to Hoyop-Hoyopan Cave.

After 11:00, when the heat builds, the water surface gets hot. There is little shade, so bring a hat and sunscreen. Walking slowly around the lake to see the village scenery is also nice. Photos look different from the shore and from a raft, so try both.

items.title: Camalig and Albay full day
items.subtitle: Lake, cave and ruins in one go

children.text: Take a jeepney or van from Legazpi to Camalig and go to Sumlang Lake first.
Tour two chambers of Hoyop-Hoyopan Cave with a guide.
Have lunch in Camalig town and try pinangat.
See Mayon and the ruins together at Cagsawa Ruins.
Return to Legazpi.

Mayon is most visible in the December–May dry season, when there are fewer clouds, and early in the morning. The 2025 guide says the dry season brings clearer skies and better Mayon views, and advises checking the weather in the rainy season.

One guide lists opening hours as 08:00–18:00 Monday to Thursday and 06:30–18:00 Friday to Sunday. Go early on weekends to avoid crowds. Both the cool, misty early morning and sunset photos in the afternoon have their charm.

There is no lodging at the lake, and most visitors stay in Camalig town or in Legazpi. Places such as Casa Simeon Heritage House are mentioned in Camalig, and Legazpi has more guesthouses and hotels. Room rates vary by date, so check a booking site.

The café by the lake reportedly serves Bicolano dishes such as laing (taro leaves simmered in coconut milk), Bicol Express and pancit Bato. Camalig town is said to have a halo-halo shop and a heritage restaurant, so it is easy to continue lunch after leaving the lake. Many local dishes use spicy coconut-milk sauces, so say so when ordering if you want to avoid spice.
Bring plenty of cash. Entrance, parking, activities and food are often paid for in cash. Buying snacks from stalls around the lake also helps local people.
Camalig is a town in Albay about
12km
from Legazpi and about
515km
from Manila. Sumlang is a small village in it, with about 2,000 residents in the 2024 census. The town's patron saint day is
June 24

(the Saint John the Baptist parish church), and a pinangat festival is reportedly held in June as well. If you visit then, you can see town events along with the lake, but lodging and transport can get crowded, so book early. Also remember that June is when the rainy season begins, so clouds may hide Mayon.
Go early on a dry-season morning to see Mayon at its best.
Weekends bring more visitors, so arrive early.
Bring cash. Entrance and activity fees are collected on site.
Always wear a life jacket on the rafts, kayaks and aqua bikes.
Keep your phone and camera in a waterproof pouch.
There is not much shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
Carry your trash out or use the designated bins. This is a place that villagers work to protect.
Swimming is reportedly not allowed, so follow the rules.
The facilities are run by local people, so ask for rates and rules on site. Staff are happy to answer questions.
The lake is small and not a place to stay long. It works best when combined with other sights in your itinerary.
Swimming is prohibited, and water activities must be done in a life jacket. Rates differ greatly by source, so check the posted rates on site.
Rates in the 2016 review and the 2025 guide are very different. Confirm the current rates at the lake entrance.
Lake activities may be limited during rain or a typhoon warning, so check the weather.
There is little shade and the midday sun is strong, so watch out for dehydration and heatstroke.
Parking space can run short on weekends.
Check whether there is an official rate list and ask for a receipt if needed.
A limestone cave in the village of Cotmon in Camalig. Its breezy openings and Mayon-facing window make it a good same-day pairing.
The remains of a church buried by the 1814 eruption of Mayon, and Albay's best-known sight, close to the lake.
The symbol of Albay and the backdrop of the lake. It is clearest on dry-season mornings.
